These are two different rights, governed by two different laws, and businesses that confuse them often leave their brand under-protected.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">Does Indian copyright law recognize AI as an author?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Not clearly, and that's the core problem. The Copyright Act, 1957 protects "original" works, and Section 2(d) defines who counts as an "author." For most works, that's the human creator. But Section 2(d)(vi) — added by a 1994 amendment, well before generative AI existed — covers "computer-generated" literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, and names the author as "the person who causes the work to be created." That phrase was written for rule-based software, not diffusion models generating an image from a text prompt. Applied to modern AI tools, it's genuinely unclear whether the human who typed the prompt "causes" the output enough to qualify as its legal author, especially when the output isn't directly controlled by the user.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">What did the RAGHAV "Suryast" case actually decide?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Less than it seems. In November 2020, the Indian Copyright Office registered an artwork called "Suryast," listing IP lawyer Ankit Sahni and an AI tool called RAGHAV as co-authors — reportedly a global first. Later, the Copyright Office issued a withdrawal notice, questioning RAGHAV's legal standing as an "author" and pointing back to Section 2(d)(vi). Sahni contested the withdrawal, and the matter has not been conclusively resolved in a way that sets clear precedent. For contrast, the US Copyright Office rejected the same work outright, holding that it lacked the human authorship copyright requires. Even India's one high-profile test case ended in ambiguity, not a settled rule.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">Can you copyright a logo an AI generated with no human creative input?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Very likely not, under current practice — but there's no definitive ruling to point to either way. The Copyright Office's practice and the Act's language both lean on human creativity as the basis for protection; a fully autonomous output with no meaningful human creative choices sits in a legal gap nobody has closed yet. The government is aware of this gap and has been examining AI and copyright policy, but no statutory amendment specifically resolving AI-output authorship had been notified as of mid-2026. Treat AI-logo copyright ownership as unsettled — not denied, and not guaranteed.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">Does an AI-generated logo still qualify for trademark protection?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Yes — and this is the part worth acting on. Trademark law under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 doesn't ask who or what "authored" a mark. Section 2(1)(zb) defines a trademark as a mark capable of graphical representation and capable of distinguishing your goods or services from someone else's. What matters is:</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg What is Amazon Brand Registry?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Amazon Brand Registry is a program designed to give brand owners control over their product listings. It verifies that YOU are the rightful owner of the brand.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Once enrolled, Amazon treats you differently. You stop being just a "Reseller" and become a "Brand Owner". The algorithm prioritizes your data over anyone else's.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">2. The "Holy Trinity" of Benefits</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Why should you bother? Because Brand Registry gives you access to three superpowers that regular sellers don't have.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Superpower #1: Protection (Stopping Hijackers)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Without Brand Registry, any seller can click "Sell Yours" on your listing. With Brand Registry, you get: Automated Protections: Amazon's AI proactively scans for infringing listings and shuts them down. Project Zero: A specialized tool that lets you remove counterfeit listings yourself without waiting for Amazon's approval. You become the judge and jury.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Superpower #2: Conversion (A+ Content)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Have you seen product pages with beautiful HD images, comparison charts, and brand stories in the description? That is A+ Content (formerly Enhanced Brand Content). Visual Storytelling: Replace boring text descriptions with rich graphics. Impact: Data shows that A+ Content increases conversion rates by up to 10-15%.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Superpower #3: Analytics (Brand Analytics)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Regular sellers fly blind. Brand Owners get X-Ray vision. Search Query Performance: See exactly what keywords customers type to find your brand. Repeat Purchase Behavior: Know how many customers are coming back for a second order.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">3. The Mandatory Requirement: A Registered Trademark</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Here is the catch. You cannot just join Brand Registry because you want to. The gatekeeper is the content of your legal trademark.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">To be eligible, you MUST have:</p><ol class="list-decimal space-y-2 pl-6 text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700 marker:font-bold marker:text-brand"><li>A Registered Trademark (®) issued by the Government of India (status must be 'Registered'). Update: In some cases, Amazon now accepts 'Pending' trademarks (Status: Application Filed) for early enrollment, but full features unlock only after registration.</li><li>A Word Mark or a Device Mark that clearly shows the brand name.</li><li>The brand name on the trademark must exact match the brand name on your product packaging.</li></ol><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The "Image" Requirement: Amazon will ask for photos of your product where the brand name is permanently affixed. Allowed: Printed on the box, stitched on the shirt, engraved on the metal. Not Allowed: A sticker pasted on a generic pouch. Amazon checks this manually to prevent fraud.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">4. Here is the roadmap.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Step 1: Get your Trademark Application Number If you haven't filed yet, stop reading and contact BookMyTM. You will get an Application Number (e.g., 6723456).</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Step 2: Sign in to Brand Registry Go to brandservices.amazon.in. Login with your existing Amazon Seller Central credentials.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Step 3: Enroll a New Brand Click "Enroll a new brand". You will need to provide: Brand Name. Trademark Registration Number. Trademark Status (Registered/Pending). Product Category. Images of Product & Packaging.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Step 4: The Verification Code (The Tricky Part) Amazon will send a verification code. They do not email it to you directly. They send it to the Attorney or the Email Address listed on the public trademark record (IP India website). Why? To prove you actually own the trademark application. Action: You need to get this code from your trademark agent and enter it into the Amazon portal.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">5. The Delhi High Court, in particular, delivered several judgements that sent a strong message to copycats: Similarity is not flattery; it is theft.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">For small business owners in Kerala, these high-profile battles might seem distant. But the legal principles established in these cases apply just as much to a bakery in Kottayam as they do to a multinational corporation.</p><h2 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Core Lesson</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">"You don't need to be a billion-dollar company to protect your brand. You just need to be First, Distinct, and Registered."</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">1. The Amul "Well-Known" Trademark Case</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">In a significant ruling, the courts reinforced the status of "Amul" as a Well-Known Trademark. Copycats selling "Amul Candles" or "Amul Hosiery" tried to argue that since Amul only sells dairy, they could use the name for other products.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The Verdict: The court said NO. A "Well-Known" mark is protected across all classes. Calculated deception to ride on a famous brand's reputation is illegal, regardless of the product category.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">2. The Crocs Shape Trademark Battle</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Can the shape of a shoe be a trademark? Crocs fought hard to protect its distinctive clog design against cheap knockoffs. The argument was about "Trade Dress"—the visual appearance of a product.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The Lesson: If your product has a unique shape (like a Coca-Cola bottle or a Toblerone bar), you can trademark the shape itself, not just the logo printed on it.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">3. What "Deceptive Similarity" Means for You</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Most small businesses get sued not for copying a name exactly, but for being "Deceptively Similar". If you name your coffee shop "Starbucks Kerala" in green font, you will lose. If you name it "Sardarbucks", you will still likely lose (as a famous case proved).</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The test is: "Would a person of average intelligence and imperfect recollection be confused?" If the answer is yes, you are infringing.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">4. Learn to recognize and avoid them.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Skipping or Rushing the Trademark Search</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The #1 most costly mistake. Failing to conduct comprehensive trademark search is like sailing in a storm without checking weather forecast—you're navigating blind.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Mistake:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Scenario: Entrepreneur thinks of great name, does quick Google search, finds nothing, immediately files application. Neglects to check official IP India database for registered marks, pending applications, and phonetic similarities.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Consequence:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Inevitable result: Examiner finds similar registered mark and issues Section 11 objection for "likelihood of confusion." Application stalled. Worse: if you've invested in branding, you might receive cease-and-desist letter forcing complete rebrand.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">How to Avoid:</h4><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Conduct Thorough Search: Use official IP India portal. The 45-class system is precise and unforgiving.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Mistake:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Scenario: Tech startup in Thiruvananthapuram develops restaurant management software. They file in Class 42 (IT Services) because they're "tech company." But the software itself is downloadable product (Class 9). They miss correct class entirely.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Consequence:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Double disaster: Examiner objects because goods/services description doesn't match class. If somehow registered in wrong class, protection is useless—competitor can use your name for similar software in correct class with no legal recourse.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">How to Avoid:</h4><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Analyze Your Business: List all current and planned goods/services separately</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Use Classification Tools: Utilize official class finder tools for precise classification</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Think Broadly: Clothing brand with website needs Class 25 (apparel) + Class 35 (retail)</span></li></ul><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Filing a Descriptive Trademark</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Your brand must be distinctive, not descriptive. Law prevents monopolizing common words other traders need to describe their products.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Mistake:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Scenario: Entrepreneur opens coffee shop in Fort Kochi, tries to trademark "Kochi Fresh Coffee."</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The Consequence:</h4><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Certain rejection: Section 9 objection for being descriptive. "Kochi," "Fresh," and "Coffee" directly describe location, quality, and product. Allowing monopoly would be unfair to other coffee sellers. Almost guaranteed rejection.</p><h4 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Spectrum of Distinctiveness:</h4><h5 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Fanciful (Best)</h5><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Invented words: "Kodak," "Xerox"</p><h5 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Arbitrary</h5><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Real words, unrelated: "Apple" for computers</p><h5 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Suggestive</h5><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Hints without describing: "Netflix"</p><h5 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Descriptive (Avoid)</h5><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">"Sweet" for sugar</p><h5 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Generic (Never)</h5><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">"Clock" for timepiece</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Filing as Individual vs. Company (Wrong Entity)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Trademark owner must be the entity actually using it in commerce. loading="eager" decoding="sync" fetchPriority="high"/><div class="space-y-5"><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">നിങ്ങളുടെ പുതിയ ബ്രാൻഡിന്റെ നിലനിൽപ്പിനുള്ള ഏറ്റവും വലിയ ഭീഷണി ഒരുപക്ഷേ നിങ്ങളുടെ എതിരാളികളോ, കഠിനമായ വിപണിയോ, അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ഫണ്ടിംഗിന്റെ അഭാവമോ ആയിരിക്കില്ല. ഏറ്റവും വലിയ ഭീഷണി ഒരുപക്ഷേ നിങ്ങൾ തന്നെയായിരിക്കും.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">ഇതൊരു കഠിനമായ പ്രസ്താവനയാണ്, പക്ഷേ ഇത് നിർണ്ണായകമാണ്. ഓരോ ദിവസവും, ഇന്ത്യയിലെ ആവേശഭരിതരും ബുദ്ധിമാന്മാരുമായ സംരംഭകർ അറിയാതെ തന്നെ തങ്ങളുടെ ബ്രാൻഡിനെ അട്ടിമറിക്കുന്ന പ്രവൃത്തികളിൽ ഏർപ്പെടുന്നു.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">തങ്ങളുടെ ബിസിനസ്സ് ആരംഭിക്കാനും വളർത്താനുമുള്ള തിടുക്കത്തിൽ, ട്രേഡ്മാർക്ക് പ്രക്രിയയിൽ അവർ വരുത്തുന്ന ലളിതവും എന്നാൽ ഒഴിവാക്കാവുന്നതുമായ പിഴവുകൾ, അവരുടെ ബ്രാൻഡിന്റെ നിയമപരമായ അടിത്തറയെ ഗുരുതരമായി ദുർബലപ്പെടുത്തുന്നു. ഇത് ബ്രാൻഡിനെ പ്രതിരോധമില്ലാത്തതും ആക്രമണങ്ങൾക്ക് വിധേയവുമാക്കുന്നു.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">ഇവ വെറും ചെറിയ പിഴവുകളല്ല; മറിച്ച് നിങ്ങളുടെ അപേക്ഷ നിരസിക്കുന്നതിലേക്കും, നിക്ഷേപം പാഴാകുന്നതിലേക്കും, നിങ്ങൾ കഠിനാധ്വാനം ചെയ്ത് കെട്ടിപ്പടുത്ത ബ്രാൻഡ് നാമം പൂർണ്ണമായും നഷ്ടപ്പെടുന്നതിലേക്കും നയിക്കാവുന്ന തന്ത്രപരമായ മണ്ടത്തരങ്ങളാണ്.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">ഈ വഴികാട്ടി നിങ്ങളുടെ "ബ്രാൻഡ് പ്രതിരോധ മാനുവൽ" ആണ്. ഏറ്റവും സാധാരണമായ ഏഴ് ട്രേഡ്മാർക്ക് തെറ്റുകൾ ഞങ്ങൾ ഇവിടെ തുറന്നുകാട്ടുകയും, അവ ഒഴിവാക്കുന്നതിനുള്ള വ്യക്തവും പ്രവർത്തനക്ഷമവുമായ പ്രതിരോധ തന്ത്രങ്ങൾ നൽകുകയും ചെയ്യും.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">"കണ്ണടച്ച് ഫയൽ ചെയ്യൽ" - ട്രേഡ്മാർക്ക് സേർച്ച് ഒഴിവാക്കുകയോ തിടുക്കത്തിൽ നടത്തുകയോ ചെയ്യുന്നത്</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">ഇതാണ് ട്രേഡ്മാർക്ക് ഫയലിംഗിലെ ഏറ്റവും വലിയ പാപം. വിനാശകരമായ പ്രത്യാഘാതങ്ങളുള്ള, ഒഴിവാക്കാവുന്ന ഒരു പിഴവാണിത്.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">തെറ്റ്:</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">ഒരു സംരംഭകൻ ഒരു മികച്ച പേര് It starts with a simple missed deadline—perhaps an oversight by an accountant or a delay in finalizing the yearly audit. But under the stringent rules introduced by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) in 2018, that minor delay triggers a relentless penalty of ₹100 per day, per form, with absolutely no upper limit.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Fast forward three or four years, and a dormant startup or a struggling small business suddenly finds itself staring at an insurmountable wall of late fees running into lakhs of rupees. For many founders, the penalty has exceeded the actual paid-up capital of the company itself, leaving them financially paralyzed and legally vulnerable.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">But on February 24, 2026, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs threw struggling businesses a massive, unprecedented lifeline.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Through General Circular No. 01/2026, the government officially notified the Companies Compliance Facilitation Scheme, 2026 (CCFS-2026). This is not just a minor policy tweak; it is a full-scale corporate amnesty program. For a strictly limited 90-day window, the government is allowing defaulting companies to wipe their slate clean, regularize their records, and escape prosecution at a fraction of the actual cost.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">If your company has pending ROC filings, this is the most important legal update of the decade. Here is exactly what CCFS-2026 means for your business, the hidden risks of ignoring it, and how to secure your fee waiver before the portal slams shut.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">The Update: Breaking Down CCFS-2026 (Simplified)</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The core objective of the Companies Compliance Facilitation Scheme 2026 is to clean up the MCA-21 registry and promote the "Ease of Doing Business" by offering a fresh start. The scheme goes live on April 15, 2026, and permanently closes on July 15, 2026.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Unlike previous schemes, CCFS-2026 is highly structured, offering three distinct "Relief Tracks" depending on the current status and future intentions of your company:</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The 90% Penalty Waiver for Active Companies</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">This is the headliner benefit that will save businesses millions. If you intend to keep your company active and operational, but you have years of pending Annual Returns (MGT-7 / MGT-7A) or Financial Statements (AOC-4 and its variants), you can now file them by paying the standard government filing fee plus only 10% of the accumulated additional late fees.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Imagine your company failed to file its AOC-4 and MGT-7 for three consecutive financial years. The standard ₹100/day penalty would have ballooned the additional fees to approximately ₹2,19,000.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Under the CCFS-2026 scheme, that ₹2,19,000 penalty is slashed by 90%. You will only pay ₹21,900 in late fees to completely regularize your company. This 90% discount applies to a wide range of forms, including ADT-1 (Auditor Appointment) and even legacy forms under the old Companies Act, 1956.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The 50% Discount for "Dormant" Status</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">What if you have a startup that has paused operations, or a holding company that isn't currently doing any active business? You don't want to close it, but you also don't want the burden of yearly compliance.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">CCFS-2026 allows inactive companies to officially apply for "Dormant" status under Section 455 of the Companies Act by filing Form MSC-1. During the scheme's three-month window, the MCA is offering a 50% discount on the normal filing fee for this form. Once dormant, your yearly compliance drops to near zero, safely parking your corporate entity for future use.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">The 75% Discount for a Clean Exit (Strike-Off)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">If your company is entirely defunct and you simply want to shut it down and walk away without legal liabilities haunting you, the MCA has drastically lowered the exit barrier. By filing Form STK-2 during the scheme period, you can voluntarily strike off your company by paying only 25% of the standard filing fee.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">The Impact: What Happens If You Ignore the July 15 Deadline?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">It is critical to understand that the CCFS-2026 is a "Facilitation" scheme, but it is immediately followed by a period of aggressive "Enforcement." The MCA is giving you a carrot now, but the stick arrives on July 16, 2026.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">If you fail to utilize this 90-day window, the consequences will be severe and immediate:</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">1. Full Reinstatement of Crushing Penalties</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">At midnight on July 15, the 90% waiver vanishes. Loss of Immunity from Prosecution</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">One of the most powerful—yet overlooked—benefits of CCFS-2026 is legal immunity. If you file your pending documents under this scheme, the MCA guarantees immunity from penalty proceedings and prosecution under Sections 92 and 137 of the Companies Act.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Note: This immunity is granted provided you file before an adjudicating officer issues a formal notice, or within 30 days of receiving such a notice.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">If you ignore the scheme, the Registrar of Companies (ROC) is fully authorized to initiate prosecution. This is not just a corporate issue; directors can be held personally liable for these compliance failures.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">3. Disqualification of Directors (DIN Freezing)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Persistent non-compliance inevitably leads to the disqualification of Directors. If your company fails to file financial statements or annual returns for three continuous financial years, the ROC will freeze your Director Identification Number (DIN). Once your DIN is disqualified, you are forced to resign from all other companies you are a director of, and you cannot incorporate a new company anywhere in India for a period of five years.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">4. The Top Reasons RUN/SPICe+ Applications Fail" width="640" height="360" class="mb-10 aspect-video w-full rounded-3xl object-cover shadow-lg" loading="eager" decoding="sync" fetchPriority="high"/><div class="space-y-5"><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Most company name applications in India get rejected for a handful of predictable reasons: the name is too similar to an existing company, LLP, or registered trademark; it uses a restricted word without government approval; or it doesn't match the business the company actually plans to do. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) checks every name against the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, and understanding those rules before you apply — not after a rejection — is the single biggest factor in getting approved on the first try.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">How does name approval actually work — RUN or SPICe+?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">You have two routes on the MCA portal. RUN (Reserve Unique Name) is a standalone web service used purely to reserve a name before you're ready to file the rest of your incorporation paperwork, or to rename an existing company. SPICe+ (INC-32) Part A is the name-reservation step built into the integrated incorporation form, which also generates DIN, PAN, TAN, and EPFO/ESIC registration once you proceed to Part B. Both let you submit up to two proposed names in order of preference, and if neither is available you typically get one resubmission attempt. Applications are checked by the Central Registration Centre (CRC), and the outcome is emailed to the applicant with reasons if rejected.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">Why does MCA reject names that are "too similar" to another company?</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Because Rule 8 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 Restricted terms commonly cited include "Board," "Commission," "Authority," "Undertaking," "National," "Union," "Central," "Federal," "President," "Rashtrapati," "Minister," "Governor," and similar words that could suggest a government, statutory, or regulatory connection. Separately, sector-specific words like "Bank," "Insurance," "Stock Exchange," or "Mutual Fund" require confirmation that relevant regulatory conditions are met before use.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl "Aren't they the same thing?"</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">This is the single most expensive mistake creative professionals make.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Trademark and Copyright are two completely different legal weapons. The Fundamental Difference</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The difference is simple if you remember this rule:</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Trademark protects your IDENTITY (Who you are).</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Copyright protects your EXPRESSION (What you created).</span></li></ul><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Trademark (The Brand Guard)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">It protects things that identify the source of a product. Examples: Brand Name (Nike), Logo (The Swoosh), Slogan ("Just Do It"), Sound Mark (Netflix "Tu-Dum"). Goal: To prevent consumer confusion.</p><h3 class="mt-8 text-xl font-bold text-gray-900">Copyright (The Content Guard)</h3><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">It protects original literary, artistic, dramatic, and musical works. Examples: Books, Songs, Movies, Paintings, Software Code, Website Design. Goal: To prevent unauthorized copying or distribution.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">2. You put it on your cups so people know the coffee is from you.</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">As an Artwork: It is a Copyright. An artist drew it. It is an artistic creation.</span></li></ul><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Q: So, which one should I file?</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">A: For most businesses, Trademark is Priority #1. Why? because Trademark protects the commercial value of the logo. Copyright only protects the artistic value. If someone opens a shop with a similar logo, a Trademark Lawsuit is much stronger and faster than a Copyright Lawsuit.</p><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Pro Tip: File Copyright for your logo ONLY if the artwork itself is extremely unique and valuable (like a painting), independent of the brand name.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">3. Design registration protects the visual features of an article — its shape, configuration, surface pattern, or ornamentation — for up to 15 years, and it is a separate right from both trademark and copyright protection.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">What qualifies as a registrable design</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">A "design" under the Act means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament, or composition of lines or colours applied to an article, whether in two or three dimensions, by an industrial process, and judged solely by the eye. To be registrable, the design must be new or original, not previously published or used anywhere, and significantly distinguishable from known designs.</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" visual appearance of a manufactured article (a bottle shape, a furniture design, a textile pattern)</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Must be new/original and not disclosed before filing</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Judged by visual appeal, not by how the article functions</span></li></ul><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">What is excluded from design protection</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Several categories cannot be registered as designs even if visually distinctive:</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" IP India</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">Design applications are filed with the Designs Wing of the Indian Patent Office (part of IP India) and classified under the Locarno Classification system, which groups articles into numbered classes. The process runs through these stages:</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full are often registered within a few months of filing.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">Validity period: 10 years, extendable by 5</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">A registered design is protected for 10 years from the date of registration. Before that period expires, the proprietor can apply to the Controller, with the prescribed fee, to extend protection for a further 5 years — giving a maximum total term of 15 years. There is no renewal beyond that; once the 15-year period lapses, the design falls into the public domain.</p><h2 class="mt-10 text-2xl font-extrabold tracking-tight text-gray-900">How this differs from trademark and copyright protection</h2><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">The same product can carry multiple, non-overlapping IP rights:</p><ul class="space-y-2.5"><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Design registration protects how an article looks — its shape and ornamentation — for up to 15 years, tied to an industrial article.</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Trademark registration protects a brand identifier — a name, logo, or in some cases a distinctive product shape used as a source indicator — and can, in principle, be renewed indefinitely.</span></li><li class="flex items-start gap-3"><span class="mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 flex-shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-brand-surface text-brand"><svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M5 13l4 4L19 7"></path></svg></span><span class="text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700">Copyright protects original artistic, literary, or creative works and generally isn't available for something once it has been registered (or is registrable) as an industrial design, though the underlying artwork before industrial application may retain copyright.</span></li></ul><p class="text-base leading-[1.8] text-gray-700">A business that wants full protection of a distinctively shaped product typically needs to consider design registration for the shape and a separate trademark filing for the brand name or logo applied to it. BookMyTM works with businesses across India to identify which of these protections actually apply to a given product and to handle the IP India filing process end to end.</p><div class="space-y-4"><div class="rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-5"><h3 class="mb-2 text-[16px] font-bold text-gray-900">How long does a registered design stay protected in India?</h3><p class="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-gray-600">Ten years from the date of registration, extendable once by five more years for a maximum of 15 years total.</p></div><div class="rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-5"><h3 class="mb-2 text-[16px] font-bold text-gray-900">Can I register both a design and a trademark for the same product?</h3><p class="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-gray-600">Yes — a design registration protects the article's shape/appearance, while a trademark protects a brand name, logo, or distinctive source-identifying feature; they serve different purposes and can coexist.</p></div><div class="rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-5"><h3 class="mb-2 text-[16px] font-bold text-gray-900">Can I register a logo or brand name as a design?</h3><p class="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-gray-600">No. Trademarks and property marks are expressly excluded from design registration and must be filed under trademark law instead.</p></div><div class="rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-5"><h3 class="mb-2 text-[16px] font-bold text-gray-900">Does design registration protect how a product works?</h3><p class="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-gray-600">No. Design law protects visual appearance only — purely functional or mechanical features dictated by function are not registrable.</p></div><div class="rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-gray-50 p-5"><h3 class="mb-2 text-[16px] font-bold text-gray-900">What happens if I don't extend my design registration after 10 years?</h3><p class="text-[15px] leading-relaxed text-gray-600">If you don't apply for the five-year extension before the initial 10-year term ends, the design loses protection and enters the public domain.</p></div></div></div></article><aside class="space-y-6 lg:sticky lg:top-28"><div class="overflow-hidden rounded-3xl bg-white shadow-xl ring-1 ring-gray-200/70"><div class="hero-bg px-7 py-6
